title: Motion in a Line and in a Plane

cards.b:
Before asking what makes things move, physics first learns to describe motion exactly. A cricket ball leaves the bat, rises, slows, turns and falls. Where is it? How fast? When does it land?

The branch that answers this is kinematics. Its tools are simple: position, velocity, acceleration and a few equations. Once you own them, you can predict where a ball, a car or a rocket will be, using nothing but arithmetic.

Speed is how fast; velocity is speed with direction. Average velocity is displacement divided by time:

Average velocity

v = change in position / change in time

If a train covers 120 km in 2 hours, its average speed is 60 km/h. But the speedometer shows instantaneous speed, the speed at one moment. On a graph of position against time, instantaneous velocity is the slope of the line at that point.

Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes:

Acceleration

a = change in velocity / time

A car going from 0 to 20 m/s in 5 s has a = 20/5 = 4 m/s squared. Every second, its speed grows by 4 m/s.

Braking is also acceleration (negative, or deceleration). So is turning a corner at steady speed, because the direction of velocity is changing. Anything that changes velocity, in size or direction, is accelerating.

When acceleration a is constant, starting speed u, final speed v, time t, distance s:

Equations of motion

v = u + a t
s = u t + (1/2) a t squared
v squared = u squared + 2 a s

On a speed-time graph the slope is the acceleration and the area under the line is the distance travelled. The equations are just this geometry written in algebra.

Near Earth's surface, anything falling freely gains about 9.8 m/s of speed every second. We call this g = 9.8 m/s squared.

Galileo (around 1600) argued that heavy and light bodies fall together; air resistance is what makes a feather lag. In 1971 on the Moon, where there is no air, astronaut David Scott of Apollo 15 dropped a hammer and a feather together. They landed at the same instant.

Gravity on the Moon is about one-sixth of Earth's, but the lesson is the same: in free fall, mass does not matter.

Throw a ball at an angle. Its motion splits into two independent parts:

  • Horizontal: no force, so constant speed.
  • Vertical: gravity pulls, so constant acceleration downwards.

Combine them and you get a curve called a parabola. For launch speed u at angle theta (level ground), the range is R = u squared x sin(2 theta) / g. This is largest at 45 degrees. Two angles that add to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60, give the same range.

cards.h: Ball thrown straight up at 20 m/s
cards.b:
Take g = 9.8 m/s squared. At the top the speed is zero, so v squared = u squared - 2 g h gives:

0 = 400 - 19.6 h, so h = 20.4 m.

Time to the top: v = u - g t gives 0 = 20 - 9.8 t, so t = 2.04 s. Coming down takes the same, so total flight is about 4.1 s.

It returns to your hand at 20 m/s, the same speed it left with, but pointing down.

• 'At the top the ball has no acceleration.' Wrong. Its velocity is momentarily zero but gravity still pulls: a = 9.8 m/s squared downward all the time.
  • 'Heavier things fall faster.' Only because of air. In a vacuum all fall together.
  • 'The ball keeps going because of a force from the bat.' After release the only force is gravity (and a little air drag).

ISRO launches most satellites eastwards from Sriharikota (about 13.7 degrees north). The Earth spins eastwards, giving the launch pad a free speed of roughly 450 m/s, so the rocket needs less fuel to reach orbital speed. This is the same idea as adding velocities in vectors.

On the sports field, Neeraj Chopra won javelin gold at the Tokyo Olympics with a throw of 87.58 m. A javelin is a projectile, but it is also a glider, so the best angle is not exactly 45 degrees.

• Velocity is the rate of change of position; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity.
  • For steady acceleration: v = u + at, s = ut + (1/2)at squared, v squared = u squared + 2as.
  • In free fall everything accelerates at g = 9.8 m/s squared, regardless of mass.
  • A projectile's horizontal and vertical motions are independent.

Think about it

1. A ball thrown up passes you at the same height going up and down. How do the two speeds compare?
2. Why can a car going round a bend at steady 60 km/h still be accelerating?
